title: System calls and interrupts
summary: Limited direct execution: user and kernel mode, how a system call traps into the kernel, timer interrupts, and what a context switch costs.

clips.title: Crossing into the kernel
clips.question: A user program can't touch the disk. So how does read() get your bytes?

scenes.say: System calls, question one. Your program isn't allowed to touch the disk. So how does a call to read get your bytes? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: You can't touch the disk. So how does read() work?

scenes.say: The CPU runs your code in user mode, where device access and privileged instructions are forbidden. To do I/O, you ask the kernel. Read in libc is a thin wrapper. It puts the system call number in one register, and the arguments in others, then executes the special syscall instruction. That traps: the CPU switches to kernel mode, onto the kernel stack, and jumps to the entry point the kernel registered at boot. The kernel trusts nothing: it checks the file descriptor, and that the buffer really is your memory, then does the work. Return from trap drops back to user mode, with the result in a register.

nodes.label:
CPU: user → kernel mode
kernel stack

return from trap
result in rax

steps.note: User mode: no devices, no privileged instructions
libc: syscall number + arguments in registers
Trap: switch to kernel mode and stack
Jump to the handler registered at boot
Validate the fd and the user buffer
Copy the data into your buffer
Back to user mode, result in rax

scenes.say: A round trip is cheap, but not free. A trivial system call costs around a hundred to a few hundred nanoseconds: in a Linux VM, get P I D took about 280. Some calls skip the kernel entirely. Clock get time reads the time from a page the kernel maps into every process, the v D S O, in about 20 nanoseconds. And hot paths batch: one call for many operations, with read v, or io uring.

left.label: System call
left.title: ~100–300 ns round trip
left.body: Mode switch, validation, cache and TLB effects. getpid: ~280 ns in a Linux VM.

right.label: vDSO
right.title: No crossing at all
right.body: clock_gettime reads a kernel-mapped page: ~20 ns.

verdict.text: On hot paths, batch: fewer crossings, more work each.

clips.title: Getting the CPU back
clips.question: A process loops forever and never makes a system call. How does the OS get the CPU back?

scenes.say: Question two. A process spins in a loop forever, and never makes a system call. How does the operating system ever get the CPU back? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: A process spins forever. How does the OS get the CPU back?

scenes.say: Early systems were cooperative. The OS got control back only when a process made a system call, or yielded. One infinite loop, and the only fix was a reboot. Modern kernels are preemptive. At boot, they program a hardware timer to interrupt every few milliseconds. The interrupt forces the CPU into kernel mode, saves the running process's registers, and runs the kernel's handler. Now the scheduler decides: keep running this process, or switch to another.

left.label: Cooperative
left.title: Wait for a syscall or yield
left.body: One infinite loop, and only a reboot helps.

right.label: Preemptive
right.title: A hardware timer interrupt
right.body: Fires every few ms; the kernel always gets the CPU back.

verdict.text: Then the scheduler decides: keep running, or switch.

scenes.say: So there are three ways into the kernel. A system call, when the program asks. An exception, when an instruction faults, like a page fault, or a divide by zero. And an interrupt, from a device or the timer, which can arrive between any two instructions. Everything else runs directly on the CPU, at full speed. That's limited direct execution.

items.label: System call
items.title: The program asks
items.body: A deliberate trap for a service.

items.label: Exception
items.title: An instruction faults
items.body: Page fault, divide by zero, bad opcode.

items.label: Interrupt
items.title: From outside
items.body: Timer, disk, network card; between any two instructions.

items.label: The rest
items.title: Runs directly on the CPU
items.body: Full speed, until one of the three.

clips.title: The context switch
clips.question: What happens in a context switch, and why is a process switch dearer than a thread switch?

scenes.say: Question three. What actually happens in a context switch? And why does switching processes cost more than switching threads? Pause and answer out loud.

A context switch happens inside the kernel: after a timer interrupt, or when a thread blocks. The kernel saves the current thread's registers: program counter, stack pointer, general registers, and floating point state. The scheduler picks the next thread. Then the kernel restores that thread's registers and kernel stack, and returns to user mode as the new thread.

items.label: 1 · Enter
items.title: Already in the kernel
items.body: Timer interrupt, or the thread blocked.

items.label: 2 · Save
items.title: Current thread's registers
items.body: PC, SP, general and FP/SIMD state.

items.label: 4 · Restore
items.title: Next thread's registers
items.body: And its kernel stack; return to user mode.

scenes.say: Between threads of one process, that's it: the address space doesn't change. Between processes, the kernel also switches page tables, by loading a new root into C R three on x86. Without tagged TLB entries, that flushes every cached translation. With P C I D, Linux keeps them, tagged per address space. Either way, the bigger cost is indirect: the new thread starts with cold caches and TLB, which can cost more than the switch itself.

left.label: Thread switch
left.title: Same address space
left.body: Registers and stacks change; page tables don't.

right.label: Process switch
right.title: New page tables too
right.body: Load CR3. Without PCID, every TLB entry is flushed.

verdict.text: The real cost is indirect: cold caches and TLB.

scenes.say: To recap. User code runs directly on the CPU, but in user mode. A system call traps into the kernel, and back. The timer interrupt guarantees the kernel gets control back. And a context switch saves one thread's registers, and restores another's, plus page tables, between processes.

items.text: User code runs directly, in user mode.
A system call traps in, and returns out.
The timer interrupt guarantees control returns.
Switch = save, pick, restore (+ page tables).
